Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 16:00 UTC

Recording id: rf-20260325-84721-edgecases-demo
Links: Deck: https://app.redwood.com/deck/edgecases | Benchmarks: https://sheets.redwood.com/bench-edgecases | Security: https://redwood-inference.com/security.pdf

Summary: 
Short demo focused on edge cases: very long context (100k+ tokens), sustained high TPS (hundreds req/sec), streaming backpressure and timeout behaviors. Customer AtlashHealth cares about telemetry, audit logs, and predictable tail latency for real-time clinical assistant.

Topics: long context handling; KV cache and prefix caching; batching and autoscaling; streaming vs chunked outputs; backpressure, retry semantics, and timeout configs; dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs; security and compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS, VPC).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, i have Priya our SE and Samir product on the call. could you do quick intros?
[00:08] Maya Thompson: sure, maya here, cto at atlashealth, overseeing platform and infra. we want to understand how redwood handles worst-case inputs, basically clinical notes with long context and high concurrency.
[00:20] Eli Ruiz: eli, ml eng, i'll run the bench and integrate the sdk. we've got requirements for per-patient full history recall ~50k tokens plus some larger attachments.
[00:30] Priya Desai: awesome. quick note, i'll demo both api + console, show optimize recommendations and a streaming scenario with backpressure. i should flag, some product names in the docs are old - you may see "Redwood Optimise" spelled two ways in notes, ignore that.
[00:45] Dana Park: dana, site reliability, interested in tail latency and retry behavior when our downstream clients slow.
[00:54] Jordan Lee: perfect. we started with a short overview then live demo.

[02:15] Priya Desai: (screenshare) first, long-context: we support pinned KV cache and prefix caching; for 50k tokens we recommend using our segmented KV approach and streaming with chunked generation to keep memory predictable. when you hit 100k+ tokens you want to consider model truncation strategies or our "context sharding" pattern.
[02:40] Eli Ruiz: quick q: will the kv cache survive model switches during rollouts? we might change quantized variants.
[02:48] Priya Desai: yes, we keep cache compatibility for compatible model variants; if the architecture changes (e.g., moving from opt-like to llama-like) you'll need to rewarm caches. also note - quantized kernels can change tokenization edge cases, sometimes you see slight off-by-one in token boundaries, it's rare but we've seen it in testing.
[03:12] Maya Thompson: that's fine, as long as we can detect regressions. we need alerts on quality regressions tied to prompt sets.

[05:00] Priya Desai: next, high TPS: our Dedicated offering gives reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policies. we've run benchmarks at sustained 400 rps with batching and smart routing. in hosted, bursting above certain thresholds will route to fallback models or queue with a backoff.
[05:25] Dana Park: and what about per-tenant isolation? we can't have noisy neighbors affecting latency.
[05:30] Jordan Lee: Dedicated provides physical isolation; in hosted we use tenant-aware scheduling and soft isolation but for strict isolation you'd pick Dedicated or Private VPC.

[08:10] Priya Desai: demoing the console: here's the per-route dashboard, token-level latency breakdown, and per-model SLO charts. you can set automatic fallback policies - e.g., if tail p95 goes above 800ms, route to a lower-cost variant.
[08:35] Eli Ruiz: do you expose the batching window config via API? we want programmatic control.
[08:40] Priya Desai: yes, batching/window and max batch size are configurable at route level and via SDK. note that aggressive batching reduces cost but increases latency; we surface recommended settings in Optimize based on your workload.

[12:20] Priya Desai: now streaming/backpressure: for streaming responses we open a single HTTP/2/WS stream and push tokens. if the client is slow, we apply backpressure logic - we can pause generating tokens, buffer up to a configurable limit, or spill to a cache. default behavior is to apply flow-control and send a 429-like signal to the caller after backpressure thresholds.
[12:50] Eli Ruiz: so timeouts then - what's the retry semantics? if we get a client timeout mid-stream, do you finish generation server-side?
[12:58] Priya Desai: by default we cancel generation to free GPU for other work, but you can enable a "continue-on-timeout" mode where the server completes generation and stores the result in an async object you can poll. that mode increases GPU consumption and costs.
[13:20] Samir Khan: also, we have a streaming checkpointing feature - partial KV saves so even if streaming is interrupted you don't lose session state. it's in beta.

[15:45] Speaker 1: (mumble) i heard something about chunking the context, can you explain the sharding again?
[15:52] Priya Desai: sure - context sharding splits the long document into overlapping windows, runs shortened attention over shards and merges results via a secondary aggregator model. it's more compute but keeps per-request memory and latency bounded.

[18:30] Maya Thompson: about SLA - we need guarantees for p99 latency under our peak load of 200 rps. is that realistic?
[18:40] Jordan Lee: on Dedicated yes, we can commit to throughput and target p99 ranges with reserve capacity and autoscale policies; p99 depends a lot on your batching policy and model choice. we'll include sample SLO numbers in the proposal.

[22:00] Eli Ruiz: there's also streaming backpressure with our internal client, it tends to block threads. do you support non-blocking clients?
[22:08] Priya Desai: our SDK supports async streaming and backpressure-aware clients; the JS and Python SDKs expose async iterators. we recommend using those for high-tps scenarios.

[25:30] Dana Park: security: we need SSO (SAML), RBAC, audit logs, KMS key control and optional HSM. and data residency - some records must stay in eu-west-1.
[25:45] Jordan Lee: understood. Redwood Private gives customer-managed VPC and KMS integration, SOC2 and ISO artifacts are available - jordan will share. note that there is an on-prem package for fully air-gapped deployments.
[26:05] Liam O'Connor: for KMS, do you support bring-your-own-key?
[26:10] Priya Desai: yes, BYOK is supported for Private and Dedicated via our KMS connectors; for hosted we offer managed keys but can integrate with cloud KMS.

[29:00] Priya Desai: live stress test: i'm going to run a simulated workload - long-context 60k tokens per request, sustained 300 rps for 2 minutes, streaming turned on. watch the dashboard for backpressure and queue depth.
[29:18] (typing / brief pause)
[29:30] Priya Desai: okay load starting... you can see CPU/GPU metrics rising, batching increases, average latency moves up but p95 stays within configured window. at ~45 seconds we start to see queued requests and we hit our streaming buffer threshold; the system sends backpressure signals and we begin dropping to fallback model for non-critical routes.
[30:10] Eli Ruiz: hmm in our stack dropping to fallback will break session quality. can we instead queue with graceful degration?
[30:16] Priya Desai: yes, you can configure "degrade to cached response" or "queue and slow-path" - it's a policy per route. if you need per-request guarantees, configure reserved capacity and burst pools.

[32:45] Maya Thompson: pricing question - for continued generation after timeout (the continue-on-timeout mode), are we billed?
[32:52] Jordan Lee: yes, billed on GPU time plus token compute; we'll call that out explicitly in the proposal - there is also a cheaper async completion storage tier.

[35:00] Speaker 2: slight audio glitch (unintelligible)
[35:05] Priya Desai: (laughs) yeah sorry there was a small hiccup, sometimes the streaming telemetry in the demo lags a bit, that's unrelated to infra.

[37:20] Priya Desai: we also demo Optimize: it analyzes historical traces and recommends batching, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles. for long-context heavy workloads it suggested our 4-bit quantization + per-route cache TTL of 24h on prefix keys.
[37:45] Eli Ruiz: any impact on hallucinations with quantization?
[37:50] Priya Desai: small risk - Optimize flags model/quantization combos with expected delta on quality; you can gate rollouts behind eval sets so you don't regress in production.

[40:10] Dana Park: about logging - we need audit logs at token/route level but not PII. can we redact at ingestion?
[40:18] Jordan Lee: yes, we support ingestion-time redaction rules and token-level sampling to avoid storing sensitive spans. we'll share the audit log schema in the security pack.

[43:00] Maya Thompson: okay quick recap and next steps?
[43:05] Jordan Lee: recap - 1) we'll send pricing + Dedicated pilot options, 2) Priya will share bench scripts and results, 3) Liam gets the SOC2/KMS docs, 4) plan pilot kickoff week of 2026-04-06.
[43:20] Maya Thompson: sounds good. can we get a short runbook for handling streaming timeouts in our app?
[43:27] Priya Desai: yes we'll include a 1-pager with recommended client patterns and SDK snippets.

[50:00] Jordan Lee: any final q's?
[50:05] Eli Ruiz: one last - compatibility with our on-prem inference? we might keep some sensitive workloads in-house but want unified SDK.
[50:12] Jordan Lee: hybrid is common - we provide the same API surface across Hosted/Dedicated/Private so your client code stays the same and you can route per-policy.
[50:25] Maya Thompson: great, thanks everyone.
[50:30] (call ends, small chatter)
